overview: This map label fits Antigonid Macedonia and the network of Greek allies led by its kings around 200 BCE. The late-third-century Hellenic alliance was a coalition, not one uniformly governed country. The imported outline also sweeps across islands and places whose relationships with Macedon varied. Its 200 to 100 BCE interval extends beyond the monarchy’s defeat in 168 BCE.

periods.title: Macedon and its allied coalition
periods.summary: Antigonus Doson’s late-third-century alliance linked Macedonian power with Greek partners.

periods.title: The last Antigonid generations
periods.summary: Macedonia remained a kingdom under Philip V and then Perseus before Rome defeated the monarchy.

items.text: Antigonus Doson’s alliance, formed around 224/223 BCE, grew from cooperation with the Achaean League against Sparta. Historian Graham Shipley describes it as a means of exercising power through other political communities. Its members retained identities and institutions of their own; a single map colour cannot display all those relationships.

A treaty fragment from Dion records Philip V and the people of Lysimacheia promising not to ally with enemies of the other party. Oaths invoked gods, including Zeus and the gods of Samothrace. The broken inscription preserves a real negotiated relationship behind the map’s broad label.

Polybius explains how several ranks of long pikes projected ahead of a Macedonian phalanx. He also stresses its need for suitable ground and the danger of losing formation. This was coordinated work by many soldiers, whose effectiveness depended on terrain and teamwork rather than weapon length alone.

Pella’s Agora combined buying, selling, production and administration around a large central court. Excavators found workshops alongside shops and official premises. The capital’s marketplace was a working neighbourhood as well as a space where people met.

Sawn animal bones help identify butcheries in Pella’s Agora. Other rooms contained narrow jars for perfumes and aromatic oils. Excavated rubbish and containers let archaeologists distinguish businesses whose signs and shopkeepers’ voices have disappeared.

Clay sealings from papyrus documents were found in Pella’s city archive. The fragile writing materials have not all survived, but the seals preserve traces of organised paperwork. Running a kingdom required records as well as royal speeches.

A silver drachma of Philip V in the Walters Art Museum, catalogued to 220 to 179 BCE, carries ΒΑΣΙΛΕΩΣ ΦΙΛΙΠΠΟΥ, “of King Philip”. This is an attested ancient Greek coin legend, given in modern transcription. The tiny inscription put royal authority into everyday circulation.

sections.title: Baths, exercise and hopes for health

items.text: Pella had a public bath in use from the last quarter of the fourth century to the end of the second century BCE. A channel for heating beneath the floor was added toward the end of that span. The warm-floor improvement belongs to the later building history, not automatically to Philip V’s reign.

Researchers interpret one room in the palace palaestra as a training space with suspended leather bags filled with sand. They were something like punching bags. The complex served the royal household and its young attendants, so this evidence describes courtly training rather than a school available to every child.

A votive inscription from the first half of the second century BCE identifies a Pella sanctuary with Darron, a deity associated with prayers for sick people. This is evidence of seeking divine help in illness. It does not establish that the sanctuary’s rituals could cure disease.

The sanctuary complex included courtyards, a horseshoe-shaped fountain and a cistern. Excavators also recovered figurines and a small altar in a room used for offerings. Water, gathering places and gifts all formed part of the setting in which worshippers sought help.

At Dion, a marble dedication names Philip V as a donor to Zeus Olympios. It was later reused in a house. The king’s name dates the inscription only to his reign, 221 to 179 BCE; its exact occasion is unknown. The fragment shows royal participation in an important Macedonian sanctuary.

An earlier Hellenistic tomb at Pella, dated to the early third century BCE, shows figures interpreted as philosophers and a central man with a celestial sphere. The sphere has prompted an identification as an astronomer. This older monument records an interest in intellectual identity before the map’s selected period.

ending.text: Rome defeated King Perseus at Pydna in 168 BCE and ended the Antigonid monarchy. Macedonia was reorganised, and a Roman province followed in 148 BCE. Cities, workshops and religious life continued after the royal government disappeared. The map’s 100 BCE endpoint should not be mistaken for the end of an independent Macedonian kingdom.
